lessons.title: Profit vs Cash: Why a Profitable Business Can Still Go Bust

children.text: Rakesh runs Shakti Corrugators, a corrugated box maker in Rajkot. In March he signs the biggest contract of his life: a large FMCG company will buy ₹60 lakh of boxes every month, double his current sales. His accountant confirms the new business is solidly profitable. Ninety days later, Rakesh cannot pay his workers' wages on time. Nothing went wrong with the order. Nobody cheated him. His business was making more profit than ever, and it still nearly ran out of money. This lesson explains exactly how that happens, and why it happens to good businesses all the time.

body.text: Profit tells you whether a business makes money. Cash tells you whether it survives long enough to collect it. Salaries, suppliers and banks are paid in cash, never in profit.

children.text: Profit and Cash Measure Two Different Things
Indian companies prepare their profit and loss statement on an
accrual basis
. A sale counts as revenue the moment goods are delivered and invoiced, even if the customer pays three months later. An expense counts when it is incurred, even if the bill is paid next quarter.

markDefs.definition: An accounting method that records income when it is earned and expenses when they are incurred, regardless of when cash actually changes hands. The Companies Act, 2013 requires companies to keep their books this way.

children.text: Cash is simpler and far less forgiving. It is the money that actually lands in, or leaves, your bank account. A ₹60 lakh invoice raised on 30 April adds ₹60 lakh to April's revenue and exactly zero rupees to April's bank balance.

columns.label: Profit
points: Recorded when a sale is invoiced or an expense is incurred
Shown in the profit and loss statement
Ignores loan principal repayments and the purchase price of machines
Answers: is this business model making money?

columns.label: Cash
points: Recorded only when money moves in or out of the bank
Shown in the cash flow statement and the bank statement
Has no non-cash items at all
Includes every EMI, capex cheque and tax payment
Answers: can we pay salaries and suppliers this month?

children.text: Worked Example: How Shakti Corrugators Ran Out of Cash
Here are the facts of Rakesh's business. The company is fictional, but the pattern is one that bankers in every Indian industrial cluster will recognise.
Before April:
sales of ₹30 lakh a month. Customers pay 90 days after invoice, so January, February and March invoices are all still unpaid on 1 April.
From April:
the new contract doubles sales to ₹60 lakh a month, also on 90-day credit terms.
Raw material (kraft paper):
60% of sales, paid to the paper mill 30 days after purchase.
Fixed costs (wages, rent, power):
₹8 lakh a month, paid in the same month.
Cash in the bank on 1 April:
₹12 lakh. To keep things simple, ignore GST and income tax for now.
Monthly profit at ₹60 lakh of sales is ₹60 lakh minus ₹36 lakh of material minus ₹8 lakh of fixed costs, which is ₹16 lakh. Every single month is profitable. Now follow the cash.

body.caption: Shakti Corrugators: profit vs cash, April to July (₹ lakh)

children.text: Read the June row slowly. Shakti has earned ₹48 lakh of profit since April, yet it needs ₹12 lakh it does not have. Customers are still paying for the old, smaller March sales, while the paper mill already wants paying for the new, bigger May purchases. The cash from the big contract only starts arriving in July.

body.text: Growth eats cash. Every extra rupee of sales on credit means you pay for materials and wages today and collect weeks or months later. Bankers call a business that grows faster than its cash can support "overtrading". It is one of the most common ways a genuinely profitable Indian SME ends up defaulting on its bank limits.

body.title: Negotiate 60 days instead of 90
body.prompt: Suppose Rakesh had negotiated 60-day payment terms with all his customers instead of 90. Everything else stays the same: ₹12 lakh opening cash, paper paid in 30 days, ₹8 lakh fixed costs, ₹30 lakh monthly sales before April and ₹60 lakh from April. What would Shakti's closing cash balance be at the end of June, in ₹ lakh?
body.explanation: With 60-day terms, each month collects the sales from two months earlier. April collects February (30) and pays 26, closing at 16. May collects March (30) and pays 44, closing at 2. June collects April (60) and pays 44, closing at 18. Profit is identical in both cases, ₹16 lakh a month. Thirty days of credit terms alone turn a ₹12 lakh shortfall into an ₹18 lakh surplus.

children.text: Five Reasons Profit and Cash Drift Apart
Credit sales are the biggest culprit, but not the only one. These are the five gaps you will meet again and again in this course.
Customers pay later than you invoice.
Revenue and profit are booked on the invoice. Cash arrives on the payment date. The unpaid amount sits on the balance sheet as
trade receivables

markDefs.definition: Money customers owe the business for goods or services already delivered and invoiced. Often called debtors in Indian SMEs.

children.text: Stock is bought before it is sold.
Buying ₹20 lakh of raw material drains ₹20 lakh of cash today, but it becomes an expense only when the finished goods are sold. Until then it sits in inventory.
Machines are paid for upfront but expensed slowly.
A new machine is paid for in one go, but the profit and loss statement only shows a small slice of its cost each year as
depreciation

markDefs.definition: The portion of an asset's cost charged as an expense each year over its useful life. It reduces profit but involves no cash payment in that year.

children.text: Loan principal is not an expense.
Only the interest portion of an EMI reduces profit. The principal repayment is pure cash out, invisible in the profit figure.
Taxes run on their own calendar.
Advance tax is due in instalments by 15 June, 15 September, 15 December and 15 March, based on the profit you expect for the year, whether or not your customers have paid you.

body.title: Show me why a ₹1 crore machine barely dents profit

children.text: Shakti buys a new corrugation line for ₹1 crore in cash. Assume it depreciates the machine over 10 years on a straight-line basis, ignoring any residual value.
Cash out in year 1:
₹1 crore, all on the day of purchase.
Depreciation expense in year 1:
₹1 crore ÷ 10 = ₹10 lakh.
Effect on year 1 profit:
down by only ₹10 lakh.
Effect on year 1 cash:
down by the full ₹1 crore.

For the next nine years the reverse happens. Profit keeps falling by ₹10 lakh a year for depreciation while no cash goes out for the machine at all. That is why depreciation is added back when you convert profit into cash flow.

body.latex: \text{Operating cash flow} \approx \text{Net profit} + \text{Non-cash expenses} - \text{Increase in working capital}
body.caption: A simplified bridge from profit to cash. Lesson 1.3 walks through the full version.

body.text: GST makes the gap wider, not narrower. For a sale of goods, GST generally becomes payable when you raise the invoice, not when the customer pays. A monthly filer typically settles the output GST on April's invoices, net of input tax credit, by 20 May. For Shakti, that is tax on sales whose cash will not arrive until July.

body.title: Profit up, cash flat
body.question: Which of these events increases a company's profit this month but adds nothing to its bank balance this month?
options: Receiving a ₹50 lakh term loan from the bank
A customer paying an invoice raised last quarter
Delivering and invoicing ₹10 lakh of goods on 60-day credit
Paying ₹5 lakh cash for a new delivery van
body.explanation: A credit sale is booked as revenue, and therefore profit, the day it is invoiced, but the cash arrives 60 days later. A loan adds cash but is not income. Collecting an old invoice adds cash but the profit was already counted last quarter. Buying a van reduces cash immediately and hits profit only gradually through depreciation.

body.title: The non-cash expense
body.textWithBlank: Depreciation reduces a company's profit, but it does not reduce its ___ in that year.
body.explanation: Depreciation spreads the cost of an asset already paid for across its useful life. No money leaves the bank when depreciation is charged, which is why it is added back to profit when working out operating cash flow.

children.text: This Is Not a Textbook Problem in India

body.label: Delayed payments owed to Indian MSMEs
body.context: Estimated as of March 2024 in the Delayed Payments Report 3.0 by GAME, FISME and C2FO, down from a peak estimate of ₹10.7 lakh crore in 2022. That is money already earned and counted as profit, still waiting to become cash.

children.text: The government has stepped in because the problem is so widespread. Under Section 15 of the MSMED Act, 2006, a buyer must pay a micro or small enterprise supplier within the agreed period, capped at 45 days, or within 15 days if there is no written agreement. Section 37(2)(g) of the Income-tax Act, 2025 (earlier Section 43B(h) of the Income-tax Act, 1961) adds teeth: if a buyer pays late, it cannot claim that expense as a tax deduction until the year it actually pays. Lesson 3.2 covers what this means for your payables.

body.text: Cash flow is not just the finance team's job. The sales head who agrees to 120-day terms, the procurement manager who bulk-buys six months of stock for a discount, and the HR team that onboards 30 people before a project bills, all move the company's cash more than any accounting entry does.

body.title: The big client and the hiring plan
body.scenario: You lead HR at a 120-person IT services company in Pune. Sales has just signed a ₹4.2 crore a year contract with a large private bank, billed monthly at ₹35 lakh, with payment 120 days after each invoice. Delivery needs 25 new engineers at an average cost to company of ₹1 lakh a month each, all joining on the 1st of next month. The CEO calls it "our most profitable deal ever" and wants offer letters out this week.
body.prompt: Before you release the offer letters, what cash questions would you raise, and with whom?
body.modelAnswer:
1. Size the gap. The new team costs about ₹25 lakh a month from month 1. The first ₹35 lakh invoice goes out at the end of month 1 and is paid around month 5. So roughly four months of payroll, about ₹1 crore, must be funded before the first rupee arrives.
2. Add the statutory outflows. Employer PF contributions are due by the 15th of the following month and TDS on salaries by the 7th of the following month, so the cash leaves on a fixed calendar regardless of client payments.
3. Ask the finance or treasury team where the ₹1 crore comes from: existing cash, an overdraft or working capital limit, or delaying other spending.
4. Ask sales whether the terms can improve: a mobilisation advance, milestone billing or 60-day terms would shrink the gap sharply.
5. Propose staggered joining dates matched to project ramp-up instead of all 25 on day one.
6. Confirm the bank's invoice approval process. A 120-day clock that only starts after a slow approval is really a 150-day clock.

children.text: Check a Real Company Yourself
For any listed Indian company you can compare profit and cash in under five minutes. Try it with the company you work for, if it is listed, or a well-known name you follow.

body.title: Profit vs cash on screener.in
steps: Open screener.in and search for the company.
In the Profit & Loss section, note Net Profit for each of the last five years and add them up.
In the Cash Flows section, note Cash from Operating Activity for the same five years and add them up.
Compare the two totals. Over several years, a healthy business usually turns most of its profit into operating cash.
If the cash total is far below the profit total, open the Balance Sheet and check whether receivables or inventory have grown much faster than sales.
Write one sentence explaining the gap in your own words.

cards.definition: Revenue earned minus expenses incurred in a period, recorded on an accrual basis regardless of when cash moves.
The actual money coming into and going out of the bank account in a period.
Recording income when earned and expenses when incurred, not when cash is received or paid.
Money customers owe for goods or services already invoiced. Profit is booked, cash is still pending.
A yearly expense spreading an asset's cost over its useful life. It cuts profit but uses no cash that year.
Growing sales faster than the business's cash can fund the extra stock, receivables and costs.

points: Profit is recorded when sales are invoiced and expenses incurred. Cash is recorded only when money actually moves.
A business pays salaries, suppliers, banks and taxes in cash, so a profitable company can still default.
Credit sales, stock purchases, machine purchases, loan principal and tax payments all pull cash and profit apart.
Fast growth on credit terms consumes cash before it produces any. Shakti earned ₹48 lakh of profit while its cash fell by ₹24 lakh.
Payment terms are a cash lever. Cutting customer credit from 90 to 60 days turned Shakti's June shortfall into a surplus.
Decisions in sales, procurement and HR move cash as much as anything the finance team does.

body.text: Shakti Corrugators and the Pune IT services company are fictional examples used for illustration. Tax and statutory due dates are simplified and can change. Confirm current rules with your chartered accountant or finance team before acting on them.
